body.x: PromLabs Inc., led by CEO Danny Kang, was founded in August 2021 and specializes in AI transformation (AX) of content production workflows. Its AI CREATIVE OS, CREUS, links the five stages of conventional production (planning, production, review, approval and archive), so the same staff can produce more content at consistently high quality. After producing more than 500 AI ad campaigns itself, the company concluded that adopting isolated AI tools cannot clear the bottlenecks in production, and it built a dedicated platform that moves the production workflow itself onto AI.

CREUS AI, aimed at B2B customers, uses an AI producer, CREW, to help with every step from organizing the brief to building scene- and cut-level storyboards and choosing the best AI model. Images take 10 times the credits and cost of text, and video takes 1,000 times as much, so CREUS lets users preview scenes in pre-visualization before generating costly video and checks quality with Agentic QA, which cuts unnecessary spending. Its Creative Intelligence Layer also remembers brand and project context, keeping each cut's faces and product colors and shapes consistent. As a result, the company said, production costs fall 60% to 70% compared with conventional shoots, and a process that took four weeks takes three days.

CREUS Go serves small business owners who lack production staff. It builds a brand DNA from store information, Smartstore and social media links and automatically generates an annual content calendar. It automates everything from content generation to social media uploads and Meta ad integration, cutting operating costs by up to 88% compared with agency fees and raising content reach by 78%. PromLabs was selected as a smart-store technology supplier for the Small Enterprise and Market Service and secured 20 annual contracts with small businesses. It has also been selected for TIPS, drawn investment from Honest Ventures and the Gyeonggi Center for Creative Economy & Innovation, and holds six registered patents with eight more pending and an IP valuation of KRW 1.3 billion (about USD 981,000).

PromLabs has made the United States its first target market. It presented in the agentic AI category at K-AI Tech Week in Silicon Valley and is discussing a promotional content collaboration and a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Lam Family College of Business at San Francisco State University (SFSU). With support from Korea's export voucher program, it is developing English and Japanese versions, and it plans to widen its global partnerships through CES 2027, the Gyeonggi Startup Summit and SLUSH 2026 in Helsinki, Finland. With its own AI influencer, Hari Kang, and a preview of its AI short-drama platform, TRIPLIX, it is also targeting the global market for content that blends K-culture with AI-driven formats.

Since moving into the Gyeonggi Startup Campus in Pangyo in August 2026, PromLabs has drawn on interpretation and translation support from the Gyeonggi Business & Science Accelerator (GBSA) and on Pangyo's IT and content network. It plans to keep adding use cases for its technology, building on collaboration with local companies and exposure from global media interviews.

AVING News met with PromLabs CEO Danny Kang at the Startup Campus in Pangyo Techno Valley to discuss CREUS, the AI CREATIVE OS that moves content production workflows onto AI, why finishing a commercial video takes more than generating one, how CREUS Go automates content and social media for small business owners, and PromLabs' plans for the U.S. market and AI short-form content. Reporter Thomas Laksoe Frederiksen conducted the interview.
Q1. Please introduce yourself and PromLabs.

A1. I'm Danny Kang of PromLabs. We provide tools that help production companies that have always made content the traditional way do AX, or AI transformation, for their workflows. The service we run is called CREUS.
Q2. How does AX work in content production, given how much AI content is already out there?
A2. CREUS is aimed mainly at B2B customers. We also run our own internal team that makes AI content. To solve the problems that team ran into, we built our own platform.
Q3. You have made more than 500 AI campaigns yourselves. What did you learn from that work?

A3. We even built some internal services to improve prompts and used them ourselves. But even with AI, people were still the bottleneck in many places. For every scene, someone entered one prompt, checked one result, and then a person reviewed that result again. We said we had adopted AI, but we weren't getting the performance we expected. So CREUS puts the way a B2B production organization works onto the platform, from planning and generation to review and even client approval.
Q4. Let's say I'm a client and I come to you with an idea for a video. How does it work, from the idea to the final video?

A4. First, anyone can generate what they want with AI today. But finishing a commercial video is a completely different matter. A video has to go through all those earlier steps, including client approval, before it reaches consumers. So we think generation and completion are very different things. If a client comes to us, we can produce the video for them on our platform, or they can use the platform directly. If they use it directly, they enter their idea for the video. Based on that, the platform casts the characters and analyzes the content scene by scene and cut by cut, and it keeps working with the user on the result they want. The user has to approve the plan before moving to the next step. After that, the platform doesn't make one result per prompt. It visualizes all the scenes and cuts at once.
Q5. Why is making content with AI more expensive than people expect?

A5. It comes down to the video stage. If text costs 1, an image costs about 10 and a video costs about 1,000. That's a big difference. Most platforms generate a result each time you enter a prompt, so people keep revising at the video stage to get it good enough for commercial use. Credits are then used up very quickly. So we moved the basis for that judgment to the front. We do a lot of work at the pre-visualization stage to improve cost efficiency.
Q6. Your service works at the brief, storyboard and production stages, and CREW, your AI producer, even reads the brief and checks the plan. What is the idea behind that?

A6. We focus on getting users from planning, to generation, to the final result. Users come to these platforms because they want a final result. Our role is to guide them to that destination as efficiently and quickly as possible.
Q7. What is the difference between CREUS AI and CREUS Go?

A7. CREUS AI, as I said, is our AI content production service for B2B customers. I started offering AI content services in early 2023, and requests for lectures and training came in, and they still do. I had several chances to teach AI content to small business owners. I found that their situations were often less ideal than I expected. One owner told me, "We take a customer every 30 minutes to cut hair. When would we have time to learn AI, make content the way we want, post it to our channels and keep managing it? That's not realistic." Once they are trained, they do very well. But many of the small business owners I met just couldn't spend the time. So I decided to offer a fully automated service where people aren't the bottleneck. That is CREUS Go.

Users give us basic information, such as their Smartstore or Naver Place link, Instagram and website. From that, CREUS Go builds the brand DNA of the business and creates an annual content calendar. Then it delivers content every month by theme. With extra features, users can also automate uploads to social media and connect Meta ads automatically.
Q8. Who are the customers using these services?

A8. For CREUS AI, we mostly serve enterprise customers. First, there are traditional production companies that want to adopt AI. Second, ad agencies. More recently, there are also mid-sized companies and small startups with in-house marketing teams, even small ones. As AI advances, most of the work can be done in-house, and the cost burden is lower, so many companies want to keep that staff in-house. We serve many of them.
CREUS Go was selected as a technology supplier for the government's smart-store program, so through that program we serve many small business owners.

Q9. Your materials say AI production cuts costs by 60 to 70 percent compared with a real shoot and shortens production time from four weeks to three days. Which countries and regions are you looking at beyond Korea?

A9. I recently went on a business trip to the United States. I was lucky to meet San Francisco State University (SFSU) through the K-AI Tech Week program in Silicon Valley. That gave us a chance to work together, and we are now discussing an MOU. One video has already turned out well, and I understand it has been exhibited.

But even in the U.S., views of AI-generated content are not ideal. Opinion kept getting better, but then issues like Hollywood likeness rights and copyright came up, and from what I've heard, perception is getting worse. I actually see that as a big opportunity for a startup in Korea. Even a service that many companies and people know and use today did not start in the U.S. Korea consumes a lot of AI content, while the U.S. market feels stagnant. So our long-term target is the U.S., and that stagnation is an opportunity for us.
Q10. You are also building English and Japanese versions of CREUS. Where does that stand?
A10. We already offer an English version. As for Japan, we plan to take part in exhibitions there, so we are preparing a Japanese version as well.
Q11. Where do you see the main market for CREUS now, and what about the future?

A11. Right now, I see the main market as AI advertising. In the long term, though, I don't think anyone expected AI-generated content to improve this quickly. It keeps moving into commercial fields, and recently it has been actively used in dramas and films too.

I have often heard that companies that own IP are highly valuable and competitive. Building IP and making AI content is also relatively easy for us at PromLabs, so we are very interested in that area. Recently, as an in-house side project, we built an AI short-drama platform called TRIPLIX, and we are previewing it internally.

Q12. The real test of the market's size may be whether users adopt AI-made entertainment. You have your own platform for AI short dramas, and your own AI influencer, Kang Hari. How are you approaching that?

A12. Our service has a feature called Casting Studio, where you can create AI influencers. I have seen many cases where someone creates an AI influencer, uses it for a few pieces of content in a short period and never uses it again. We keep improving features that let brands own a model or IP and keep using it over time.
Q13. Why does owning an AI influencer matter?

A13. I founded the company in August 2021. At that time I worked with real influencers, and I felt the human risk firsthand. In 2022, I came across Stable Diffusion, and the first thing I made with it was an AI influencer. It was sensational then, but looking back, the quality was quite crude. What we called virtual influencers then has fully turned into what we now call AI influencers, and I think that market will grow very quickly.

In China, an AI actor called Pangtaozi is reportedly earning more than 50 million won (about USD 38,000) for a one-minute ad. Inside China, demand for AI dramas and short dramas is very large in the domestic market. That is a plan for the future, but in the long term we expect K-culture and AI content formats to combine and open up a global market.
Q14. What are the benefits of being at the Startup Campus in Pangyo?

A14. We moved to Pangyo this August. The best thing so far is that we have far more chances to build networks and exchange ideas with other companies than before. Not only me, but my team members are also working with various companies in Pangyo.
